literature.headline_zh: 人偏肺病毒本期文献呈现多方向研究进展
literature.lead_zh: 本期人偏肺病毒研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 设计了三种 疫苗 构建体 (HMPV_V1–V3),HMPV-V2 被确定为主要候选结构,具有优异的结构质量和稳定性、与 TLR4 受体的强预测结合亲和力以及稳健的免疫模拟结果。 [10.1371/journal.pone.0357758]

本研究旨在量化大流行后时期年龄特异性 hMPV 中和抗体 (NAb) 水平和 血清流行率。方法我们分析了先前发表的2024年6月2日至6月30日在中国东部台州市进行的社区横断面血清流行病学调查中收集的血清样本,采用多阶段、年龄分层抽样设计,并对5岁以下儿童进行额外的超抽样。结果 共有 1303 名年龄在 16 个月至 93 岁的参与者纳入研究。结论 本研究提供了 COVID-19 大流行后时期年龄特异性 hMPV NAb 模式的基于人群的证据。致谢 我们感谢研究的参与者。道德声明 道德批准和参与同意 道德批准由复旦大学机构审查委员会授予 (IRB#2024-05-1121)。该研究符合赫尔辛基宣言。COVID-19 大流行后时期针对 人偏肺病毒 的年龄特异性中和抗体水平:中国东部台州市的一项横断面血清流行病学研究。摘要背景 COVID-19 大流行改变了 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV) 在全球的流行模式。由于目前尚无获得许可的 hMPV 预防产品,因此了解群体免疫对于识别易感人群和制定预防策略至关重要。通过基于荧光的微中和测定检测血清样本的 hMPV NAb 水平,血清阳性定义为滴度 1:30。我们估计了各个年龄组的几何平均滴度 (GMT) 和 血清流行率 率。使用广义线性模型检查与 NAb 滴度相关的因素。我们还研究了 RSV 和 hMPV 特异性抗。 [10.1186/s12879-026-14417-w]
对于 RSV,每周预测误差随着缺失水平的增加而增加,但重建的季节性负担通常仍接近适用场景中观察到的总数。对于 hMPV,每周预测 RMSE 在缺失情况下约为 1-2 个百分点。 [10.1371/journal.pone.0353681]
体格检查显示轻度低氧血症的体征,伴有弥漫性湿啰音和呼气性喘息,但没有实变证据。患者的胸片显示慢性阻塞性变化。 [10.26738/poem.v4i1.28]
所提供的证据不提供任何结果、数据计数或统计结果。 [10.1016/j.anai.2026.08.027]
literature.trend_or_risk_zh: 本期研究方向以入选文献实际覆盖的临床、流行病学、宿主生态、诊断或分子监测主题为准。
literature.lead_en: This reporting window highlights the following research developments.
key_findings_en: Three vaccine constructs (HMPV_V1–V3) were designed, and HMPV-V2 was identified as the lead candidate with excellent structural quality and stability, strong predicted binding affinity to the TLR4 receptor, and robust immune simulation results. [10.1371/journal.pone.0357758]

Antibody levels were lowest among children aged 16 to < 36 months (GMT: 217, 95% CI: 159–295). The GMTs increased to 331 among children aged 3–4 years and exceeded 1000 among those aged 5–11 years, remaining elevated throughout life. [10.1186/s12879-026-14417-w]

For RSV, weekly prediction error increased with missingness level, but reconstructed seasonal burden generally remained close to observed totals in applicable scenarios. For hMPV, weekly prediction RMSE was on the order of ~1-2 percentage points across missingness scenarios. [10.1371/journal.pone.0353681]

Physical examination showed signs of mild hypoxemia with diffuse crackles and expiratory wheezing, without evidence of consolidation. The patient’s chest radiograph showed chronic obstructive changes. [10.26738/poem.v4i1.28]
The supplied evidence does not provide any results, data counts, or statistical findings. [10.1016/j.anai.2026.08.027]
literature.trend_or_risk_en: The direction of this week's research is defined by the clinical, epidemiological, ecological, diagnostic and molecular topics actually represented by the eligible publications.
literature.brief_en: This literature brief prioritizes papers published in the active reporting window and ranks them by relevance, evidence availability, study quality, recency, and independent-source convergence. Detailed study-specific evidence is retained in the article cards below.

papers.title: Epidemiology of Human Metapneumovirus Infection-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is a globally circulating respiratory pathogen. The objective of this systematic review is to evaluate the prevalence, case fatality rate, age-related severity, and seasonality of hMPV in the group of Acute Respiratory Infections (ARIs) and Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP). METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of articles on hMPV published from January 2001 to June 2025. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we systematically searched PubMed and ScienceDirect for eligible articles using strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed to estimate pooled prevalence, and subgroup analyses were conducted by study group, geographic region, COVID-19 period, and age group. RESULTS: One hundred one studies met the inclusion criteria, of which 96 contributed to the meta-analysis. The pooled global prevalence of hMPV was 6% (95% CI: 5%-7%). Prevalence estimates were highest in patients with respiratory tract infections (RTIs) patients (6%) and in South America (10%). Age-stratified analysis showed a high prevalence in children under 5 years (7%). Seroprevalence studies demonstrated low hMPV antibody prevalence in young children less than 1 year. The case fatality rate ranged from 2.5% in elderly populations to 4.4% in severe pediatric cases. hMPV mainly affects children under 2 years, with a smaller burden in older adults. Seasonal peaks were typically observed in late winter to early spring. CONCLUSION: hMPV remains an important cause of respiratory disease worldwide, with a disproportionate burden on children. The significant heterogeneity across studies and evidence of publication bias highlight the need for standardized surveillance.

elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 人偏肺病毒(hMPV)的全球汇总患病率为6%(95% CI: 5%-7%)。患病率估计值在呼吸道感染(RTIs)患者中最高(6%),在南美洲最高(10%)。按年龄分层的分析显示,5岁以下儿童的患病率较高(7%)。病例死亡率在老年群体中为2.5%,在严重儿科病例中为4.4%。hMPV主要影响2岁以下儿童,对年长者的负担较小。季节性高峰通常出现在冬末至早春。hMPV仍是全球呼吸道疾病的重要病因,对儿童的负担不成比例。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 研究间的显著异质性和发表偏倚的证据突显了标准化监测的必要性。

papers.title: Computational prediction of a multi-epitope Human Metapneumovirus vaccine candidate through integrated reverse vaccinology and pan-genomic approaches
papers.abstract: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a primary cause of global respiratory infections yet no approved vaccine currently exists. This study computationally predicts a multi-epitope vaccine candidate using a diverse dataset of 65 HMPV sequences spanning five continents. Following the screening of lead proteins for antigenicity and virulence, fifteen highly conserved MHC-I, MHC-II and B-cell epitopes were prioritized. These were integrated with a putative L7/L12 adjuvant using optimized AAY, GPGPG, and KK linkers to design three constructs (HMPV_V1–V3). Structural validation identified HMPV-V2 as the lead candidate that exhibits a Z-score of-5.24 and 87.7% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions indicating excellent stereochemical quality and structural stability. In silico docking indicated a strong predicted binding affinity between HMPV-V2 and the TLR4 receptor (energy: −969.2). Immune simulations predicted a robust adaptive response characterized by high IgG1 titers, memory B-cell maturation, and a Th1-dominant cytokine profile. Furthermore, molecular dynamics simulations suggested exceptional structural integrity for HMPV-V2, maintaining a low RMSD of 8.213 and RMSF of 0.737 throughout the simulation. Optimized in silico cloning into the pET28a (+) vector indicated a high potential for protein expression in E. While these findings provide a theoretically grounded blueprint for vaccine development, this study is entirely computational and lacks experimental validation. Further in vitro and in vivo testing is required to confirm the actual safety and immunogenicity of the proposed candidate.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to computationally predict a multi-epitope vaccine candidate for human metapneumovirus (HMPV) due to the lack of an approved vaccine for this primary cause of global respiratory infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a diverse dataset of 65 HMPV sequences spanning five continents to computationally predict a multi-epitope vaccine candidate.
analysis.methods: Following the screening of lead proteins for antigenicity and virulence, fifteen highly conserved MHC-I, MHC-II, and B-cell epitopes were prioritized and integrated with a putative L7/L12 adjuvant using optimized linkers to design three constructs (HMPV_V1–V3).
analysis.main_results: Three vaccine constructs (HMPV_V1–V3) were designed, and HMPV-V2 was identified as the lead candidate with excellent structural quality and stability, strong predicted binding affinity to the TLR4 receptor, and robust immune simulation results.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted HMPV-V2 as the lead candidate due to its structural and immunological properties, providing a theoretically grounded blueprint for vaccine development.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest a potential vaccine candidate for HMPV, which could inform future surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is entirely computational and lacks experimental validation, limiting confidence in the actual safety and immunogenicity of the proposed candidate.

analysis.summary_en: This study computationally predicted a multi-epitope vaccine candidate for human metapneumovirus (HMPV) using a diverse dataset of 65 sequences. HMPV-V2 was identified as the lead candidate with excellent structural quality and strong predicted binding affinity to the TLR4 receptor, but further in vitro and in vivo testing is required to confirm its safety and immunogenicity.

papers.title_zh: 通过集成反向疫苗学和泛基因组方法计算预测多表位 人偏肺病毒 疫苗 候选者
papers.source_body_en: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a primary cause of global respiratory infections yet no approved vaccine currently exists. This study computationally predicts a multi-epitope vaccine candidate using a diverse dataset of 65 HMPV sequences spanning five continents. Following the screening of lead proteins for antigenicity and virulence, fifteen highly conserved MHC-I, MHC-II and B-cell epitopes were prioritized. These were integrated with a putative L7/L12 adjuvant using optimized AAY, GPGPG, and KK linkers to design three constructs (HMPV_V1–V3). Structural validation identified HMPV-V2 as the lead candidate that exhibits a Z-score of-5.24 and 87.7% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions indicating excellent stereochemical quality and structural stability. In silico docking indicated a strong predicted binding affinity between HMPV-V2 and the TLR4 receptor (energy: −969.2). Immune simulations predicted a robust adaptive response characterized by high IgG1 titers, memory B-cell maturation, and a Th1-dominant cytokine profile. Furthermore, molecular dynamics simulations suggested exceptional structural integrity for HMPV-V2, maintaining a low RMSD of 8.213 and RMSF of 0.737 throughout the simulation. Optimized in silico cloning into the pET28a (+) vector indicated a high potential for protein expression in E. While these findings provide a theoretically grounded blueprint for vaccine development, this study is entirely computational and lacks experimental validation. Further in vitro and in vivo testing is required to confirm the actual safety and immunogenicity of the proposed candidate.
papers.abstract_zh: 人偏肺病毒 (HMPV) 是全球呼吸道感染的主要原因,但目前尚无批准的 疫苗。这项研究使用跨越五大洲的 65 个 HMPV 序列的多样化数据集,通过计算预测了多表位 疫苗 候选者。在筛选先导蛋白的抗原性和毒力后,优先考虑了 15 个高度保守的 MHC-I、MHC-II 和 B 细胞表位。使用优化的 AAY、GPPGG 和 KK 连接子将它们与假定的 L7/L12 佐剂整合,设计出三种构建体 (HMPV_V1–V3)。结构验证将 HMPV-V2 确定为主要候选者,其 Z 得分为 5.24,并且 87.7% 的残基位于有利的 Ramachandran 区域,表明具有出色的立体化学质量和结构稳定性。计算机对接表明 HMPV-V2 和 TLR4 受体之间有很强的预测结合亲和力(能量:-969.2)。免疫模拟预测了强烈的适应性反应,其特征是高 IgG1 滴度、记忆 B 细胞成熟和 Th1 主导的细胞因子谱。此外,分子动力学模拟表明 HMPV-V2 具有出色的结构完整性,在整个模拟过程中保持了 8.213 的低 RMSD 和 0.737 的 RMSF。经过计算机优化克隆到 pET28a (+) 媒介 中,表明大肠杆菌中蛋白质表达具有很高的潜力。虽然这些发现为 疫苗 的开发提供了理论上的蓝图,但这项研究完全是计算性的,缺乏实验验证。需要进一步的体外和体内测试来确认拟议候选药物的实际安全性和免疫原性。

papers.title: HUMAN METAPNEUMOVIRUS: AN EMERGING THREAT WITH PANDEMIC POTENTIAL
papers.abstract: H uman metapneumovirus has gained global attention due to recent upsurge in cases reported in China.International travel and trade raise concerns about the potential spread of the 1 virus to the rest of the world.Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) was first identified in 2001 and has been a common cause of acute respiratory infections.It can cause both upper and lower respiratory tract infections and affects all age groups.Infants, children, older adults and people with low immunity are at high risk and can develop complications.Morbidity and mortality remain high in high-risk groups and hospitalized 2 patients.HMPV is an RNA virus of paramyxovirus family with two main subtypes, A and B. The virus lacks a hemagglutinin-neuraminidase protein, making it unique.
papers.journal: JAIMC Journal of Allama Iqbal Medical College

papers.title: Estimating cumulative incidence from partially missing time series of respiratory viral infections
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Seasonal respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), are major contributors to global respiratory infection burden. Estimating viral incidence using real-world data (RWD) is challenging as misalignment of data collection with seasonal circulation can lead to underestimated incidence and hinder inter-study comparisons. METHODS: We developed a regression-based approach to retrospectively correct partial-season time series with contiguous missing weeks at the start or end of a season. Weekly RSV clinical incidence (per 100,000) was extracted from U.S. RWD sources (Optum® CDM and PharMetrics Plus, adults ≥65 years; Kaiser Permanente Northwest [KPNW], all ages) for seasons 2018-19 to 2023-24 and aligned to RSV‐Net hospitalization surveillance. Weekly early- and late-season missingness scenarios were created (approximately 10%, 15%, 20%, and 25% of weeks removed). Models were fit within each season using harmonic terms and the surveillance-aligned covariate. Uncertainty was quantified using moving block bootstrap 95% prediction intervals. Weekly accuracy was evaluated using RMSE and normalized RMSE, and seasonal burden reconstruction accuracy using cumulative percent error and signed difference. For hMPV, we evaluated an illustrative extension using Optum® CDM (adults ≥65 years; 2022-23 and 2023-24) and NREVSS test positivity; because positivity is bounded and depends on testing volume, we used a denominator-aware binomial/logit model (positives out of tests). RESULTS: For RSV, weekly prediction error increased with missingness level, while reconstructed seasonal burden generally remained close to observed totals in applicable scenarios. Early-season gaps were associated with larger cumulative errors than late-season gaps in Optum® CDM and PharMetrics Plus, whereas late-season median percent errors were closer to zero across missingness levels. Applicability was reduced primarily for higher early-season missingness in KPNW due to peak overlap (e.g., early 25% scenarios not applicable). For hMPV test positivity (illustrative; two seasons), weekly prediction RMSE was on the order of ~1-2 percentage points across missingness scenarios. CONCLUSION: Across multiple RSV seasons and data sources, reconstructed seasonal burden generally agreed with observed totals when missingness was confined to contiguous early- or late-season weeks and did not overlap peak activity. This approach provides a transparent method to improve the utility and comparability of partial-season respiratory virus time series. However, applicability is reduced when peak weeks are missing, and hMPV findings are illustrative given limited seasons and the use of test positivity.

Estimating viral incidence using real-world data (RWD) is challenging as misalignment of data collection with seasonal circulation can lead to underestimated incidence and hinder inter-study comparisons. Methods We developed a regression-based approach to retrospectively correct partial-season time series with contiguous missing weeks at the start or end of a season. Weekly RSV clinical incidence (per 100,000) was extracted from U.S. RWD sources (Optum ® CDM and PharMetrics Plus, adults ≥65 years; Kaiser Permanente Northwest [KPNW], all ages) for seasons 2018–19 to 2023–24 and aligned to RSV‐Net hospitalization surveillance. Weekly early- and late-season missingness scenarios were created (approximately 10%, 15%, 20%, and 25% of weeks removed). Models were fit within each season using harmonic terms and the surveillance-aligned covariate. Uncertainty was quantified using moving block bootstrap 95% prediction intervals. Weekly accuracy was evaluated using RMSE and normalized RMSE, and seasonal burden reconstruction accuracy using cumulative percent error and signed difference. For hMPV, we evaluated an illustrative extension using Optum ® CDM (adults ≥65 years; 2022–23 and 2023–24) and NREVSS test positivity; because positivity is bounded and depends on testing volume, we used a denominator-aware binomial/logit model (positives out of tests). Results For RSV, weekly prediction error increased with missingness level, while reconstructed seasonal burden generally remained close to observed totals in applicable scenarios. Early-season gaps were associated with larger cumulative errors than late-season gaps in Optum ® CDM and PharMetrics Plus, whereas late-season median percent errors were closer to zero across missingness levels. Applicability was reduced primarily for higher early-season missingness in KPNW due to peak overlap (e.g., early 25% scenarios not applicable). For hMPV test positivity (illustrative; two seasons), weekly prediction RMSE was on the order of ~1–2 percentage points across missingness scenarios. Conclusion Across multiple RSV seasons and data sources, reconstructed seasonal burden generally agreed with observed totals when missingness was confined to contiguous early- or late-season weeks and did not overlap peak activity. This approach provides a transparent method to improve the utility and comparability of partial-season respiratory virus time series. However, applicability is reduced when peak weeks are missing, and hMPV findings are illustrative given limited seasons and the use of test positivity.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在解决由于数据收集与季节性循环不一致而导致呼吸道病毒 发病率 被低估的挑战,重点关注呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV) 和 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV)。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用基于回归的方法来校正来自美国 RWD 来源(Optum® CDM 和 PharMetrics Plus,成人≥65 岁;Kaiser Permanente Northwest [KPNW],所有年龄)的 2018-19 至 2023-24 季节的部分季节时间序列数据,与 RSV-Net 住院情况 监测 保持一致。

elements_zh.main_results: 对于 RSV,每周预测误差随着缺失水平的增加而增加,但重建的季节性负担通常仍接近适用场景中观察到的总数。对于 hMPV,每周预测 RMSE 在缺失情况下约为 1-2 个百分点。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究提供了一种透明的方法来提高部分季节呼吸道病毒时间序列的实用性和可比性,其适用性降低主要是因为 KPNW 由于峰值重叠而导致早期季节缺失较高。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该方法可以增强部分季节呼吸道病毒时间序列的实用性和可比性,有助于呼吸道感染的 监测、诊断 和 治疗。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性包括在高峰周缺失时适用性降低,以及由于季节有限和使用测试阳性而导致 hMPV 结果的说明性。

papers.abstract_zh: 背景:季节性呼吸道病毒,包括呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)和人偏肺病毒(hMPV),是全球呼吸道感染负担的主要贡献者。使用真实世界数据 (RWD) 估计病毒 发病率 具有挑战性,因为数据收集与季节性循环的不一致可能导致 发病率 被低估并阻碍研究间比较。方法:我们开发了一种基于回归的方法来回顾性地纠正在赛季开始或结束时连续缺失几周的部分赛季时间序列。每周 RSV 临床 发病率(每 100,000 人)从美国 RWD 来源(Optum® CDM 和 PharMetrics Plus,成人≥65 岁;Kaiser Permanente Northwest [KPNW],所有年龄)中提取 2018-19 至 2023-24 季节,并与 RSV-Net 住院情况 监测 保持一致。创建了每周早季和晚季缺失情景(大约删除了 10%、15%、20% 和 25% 的周)。使用调和项和 监测 对齐协变量在每个季节内拟合模型。使用移动块引导 95% 预测区间来量化不确定性。使用 RMSE 和归一化 RMSE 评估每周准确性,并使用累积百分比误差和符号差评估季节性负担重建准确性。对于 hMPV,我们使用 Optum® CDM(≥65 岁的成人;2022-23 和 2023-24)和 NREVSS 测试阳性评估了说明性扩展;因为积极性是有限的并且取决于测试量,所以我们使用了分母感知的二项式/logit 模型(测试中的积极性)。结果:对于 RSV,每周预测误差随着缺失水平的增加而增加,而重建的季节性负担通常仍接近适用场景中观察到的总数。在 Optum® CDM 和 PharMetrics Plus 中,与季末差距相比,季初差距与更大的累积误差相关,而季末中位误差百分比在缺失水平上接近于零。适用性降低主要是因为 KPNW 由于峰值重叠而造成早季缺失率较高(例如,早期 25% 的情景不适用)。对于 hMPV 测试阳性(说明性;两个季节),每周预测 RMSE 在缺失情况下约为 1-2 个百分点。结论:在多个 RSV 季节和数据源中,当缺失仅限于连续的早季或晚季周且不与高峰活动重叠时,重建的季节性负担通常与观察到的总数一致。这种方法提供了一种透明的方法来提高部分季节呼吸道病毒时间序列的实用性和可比性。然而,当高峰周缺失时,适用性就会降低,并且考虑到有限的季节和测试阳性的使用,hMPV 的结果具有说明性。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在解决由于数据收集与季节性循环不一致而导致呼吸道病毒 发病率 被低估的挑战,重点关注呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV) 和 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV)。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用基于回归的方法来校正来自美国 RWD 来源(Optum® CDM 和 PharMetrics Plus,成人≥65 岁;Kaiser Permanente Northwest [KPNW],所有年龄)的 2018-19 至 2023-24 季节的部分季节时间序列数据,与 RSV-Net 住院情况 监测 保持一致。
analysis_zh.methods: 研究人员开发了一种方法来纠正部分季节时间序列数据,方法是创建早季和晚季缺失场景(删除 10%、15%、20% 和 25% 的周)并使用调和项和 监测 对齐协变量拟合模型。使用移动块引导 95% 预测区间量化不确定性,并使用 RMSE 和归一化 RMSE 进行每周预测以及累积百分比误差和季节性负荷重建的符号差来评估准确性。
analysis_zh.main_results: 对于 RSV,每周预测误差随着缺失水平的增加而增加,但重建的季节性负担通常仍接近适用场景中观察到的总数。对于 hMPV,每周预测 RMSE 在缺失情况下约为 1-2 个百分点。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究提供了一种透明的方法来提高部分季节呼吸道病毒时间序列的实用性和可比性,其适用性降低主要是因为 KPNW 由于峰值重叠而导致早期季节缺失较高。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该方法可以增强部分季节呼吸道病毒时间序列的实用性和可比性,有助于呼吸道感染的 监测、诊断 和 治疗。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性包括在高峰周缺失时适用性降低,以及由于季节有限和使用测试阳性而导致 hMPV 结果的说明性。

papers.title: Emerging Trends in the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management of Human Metapneumovirus-Associated Respiratory Infections
papers.abstract: Introduction: Human Metapneumovirus is a significant respiratory pathogen causing infections across all age groups, particularly in young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly. Despite its clinical relevance, there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for Human Metapneumovirus, necessitating further research into therapeutic and preventive strategies. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on Human Metapneumovirus infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates. Results: Studies indicate that Human Metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against Human Metapneumovirus remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. Discussion: HMPV continues to pose a substantial public health burden due to its seasonal outbreaks, clinical similarity to other respiratory viruses, and absence of specific therapies. The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Conclusion: Human Metapneumovirus continues to pose a public health challenge due to the lack of targeted treatments and vaccines. Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.

papers.title_zh: 发病机制、诊断 和 人偏肺病毒 相关呼吸道感染管理的新趋势
papers.source_body_en: Introduction: Human Metapneumovirus is a significant respiratory pathogen causing infections across all age groups, particularly in young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly. Despite its clinical relevance, there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for Human Metapneumovirus, necessitating further research into therapeutic and preventive strategies. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on Human Metapneumovirus infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates. Results: Studies indicate that Human Metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against Human Metapneumovirus remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. Discussion: HMPV continues to pose a substantial public health burden due to its seasonal outbreaks, clinical similarity to other respiratory viruses, and absence of specific therapies. The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Conclusion: Human Metapneumovirus continues to pose a public health challenge due to the lack of targeted treatments and vaccines. Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.
papers.abstract_zh: 引言:人偏肺病毒(HMPV)是一种重要的呼吸道病原体,可在不同年龄段人群中引发感染,尤其是在幼儿、免疫功能低下者及老年人中。尽管其具有重要的临床意义,但目前尚无获批的抗病毒药物或针对人偏肺病毒的特异性治疗方法,亟需进一步研究治疗和预防策略。方法:通过系统性文献综述,检索同行评议期刊、临床试验及近期研究,重点关注人偏肺病毒感染。提取并分析数据,以评估抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体、免疫调节剂及疫苗候选物的有效性。结果:研究表明,人偏肺病毒主要靶向呼吸道上皮细胞,触发免疫应答,这些免疫应答既有助于病毒清除,也会导致疾病发病机制。正在研发的治疗方法,包括融合抑制剂和蛋白酶抑制剂,显示出潜力,但仍需进一步验证。免疫调节剂和中草药可能提供支持性益处,但其对人偏肺病毒的有效性尚未得到证实。疫苗研发取得进展,多个候选疫苗已进入临床前及早期临床阶段。讨论:由于人偏肺病毒的季节性流行、与其他呼吸道病毒的临床相似性以及缺乏特异性治疗方法,该病毒继续对公共卫生构成重大负担。该病毒通过多种机制逃避免疫应答,导致疾病严重程度增加,尤其是在易感人群中。尽管目前主要采用支持性治疗,但新兴的抗病毒药物和疫苗可能为未来提供解决方案。改善诊断可及性、提高公众意识及开展针对性研究对于控制人偏肺病毒感染至关重要。结论:由于缺乏针对性治疗方法和疫苗,人偏肺病毒继续对公共卫生构成挑战。针对抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体及疫苗的持续研究对于有效疾病管理至关重要。亟需进一步临床试验以确立安全有效的治疗方案。

papers.title: Human Metapneumovirus Infection in an Elderly Patient Receiving Maintenance Hemodialysis with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): A Case Report
papers.abstract: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is an important cause of acute infections of the respiratory system affecting young children, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. Patients suffering from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) receiving maintenance hemodialysis represent a particularly vulnerable population, yet published reports describing hMPV infection in dialysis patients remain limited. A 70-year-old male with a background of COPD, hypertension, and diabetic nephropathy with a maintenance hemodialysis regimen presented with a four-day history of fever, cough with rhinorrhea, myalgias, and dyspnea. He was immunized against influenza, COVID-19, and RSV. Physical examination showed signs of mild hypoxemia with diffuse crackles and expiratory wheezing, without evidence of consolidation. The patient’s chest radiograph showed chronic obstructive changes. Triplex RT-PCR for influenza virus, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 was negative. However, a multiplex RT-PCR respiratory panel identified hMPV. He had a good response to supportive care with oxygen supplementation, bronchodilator therapy, and continuation of his scheduled hemodialysis regimen, with subsequent discharge after five days. The above-mentioned case shows how crucial it is to consider the possible hMPV infection in differentiating the cause of respiratory complaints in dialysis patients. This infection, even being a relatively mild one, can have serious consequences from the point of view of infection control in dialysis units due to close contact between patients and their frequent use of common medical devices. This observation highlights the clinical significance of hMPV infections in hemodialysis patients.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes a 70-year-old male with COPD and end-stage renal disease undergoing maintenance hemodialysis who presented with respiratory symptoms. The patient was found to be infected with human metapneumovirus (hMPV) through a multiplex RT-PCR respiratory panel, while tests for influenza, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 were negative. His symptoms included mild hypoxemia, diffuse crackles, and expiratory wheezing, with chest radiograph showing chronic obstructive changes. The study is a single case report, which limits the generalizability of the findings, but the evidence is strong given the direct identification of hMPV through molecular testing.

papers.title: Molecular surveillance of respiratory viruses among outpatients with acute respiratory infections in Yangon, Myanmar, during the 2024 rainy season
papers.abstract: Acute respiratory infections (ARI) remain a major public health problem in Myanmar, a tropical Southeast Asian country, yet comprehensive molecular surveillance data are limited. We conducted outpatient surveillance during the 2024 rainy season and characterized pathogen distribution, seasonality, and viral genetic diversity. From June–November 2024, ARI outpatients were enrolled at two Yangon hospitals. Nasopharyngeal swabs were screened by rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2. RDT-positive specimens underwent confirmation by real-time PCR (RT-PCR). RDT-negative specimens were tested using the BioFire ® FilmArray ® Respiratory 2.1 Panel (BioFire RP). Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria viruses with cycle threshold (Ct) < 32 underwent next-generation sequencing for hemagglutinin (HA) phylogenetics. Human metapneumovirus (hMPV)-positive specimens were sequenced targeting the partial F-gene for genotyping. Among 646 ARI outpatients (median age 3.7 years), at least one pathogen was detected in 548 (84.8%). Of the 331 RDT-positive specimens, influenza A(H3N2) (40.5%), RSV-A (21.5%), and influenza B/Victoria (20.2%) were most frequently detected, alongside a single A(H1N1)pdm09 case (0.3%). Of the 315 RDT-negative specimens analyzed via BioFire RP, rhinovirus/enterovirus (42.5%) and hMPV (15.2%) were the most prevalent. Co-infections were identified in 35 (15.3%) of the 229 BioFire RP-positive specimens. Influenza activity peaked in July–August, while RSV peaked in September. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that influenza A(H3N2) sequences clustered within clades J.2/J.2.1/J.2.2, B/Victoria sequences within V1A.3a.2 (primarily C.5.7), and the single A(H1N1)pdm09 sequence within C.1.9. Notably, partial F-gene sequencing of hMPV revealed a genotype shift from mixed A2/B1 in 2023 to predominantly B2 in 2024. Various respiratory viruses co-circulated during the 2024 rainy season in this setting, displaying distinct seasonal peaks for influenza and RSV. Ongoing viral genetic evolution underscores the need for sustained molecular surveillance.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted molecular surveillance of respiratory viruses among outpatients with acute respiratory infections (ARI) in Yangon, Myanmar, during the 2024 rainy season. The research aimed to characterize pathogen distribution, seasonality, and genetic diversity. Nasopharyngeal swabs were tested using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and real-time PCR (RT-PCR) for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2. RDT-negative specimens were analyzed with the BioFire ® FilmArray ® Respiratory 2.1 Panel (BioFire RP). The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational design and potential limitations in pathogen detection.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 急性呼吸道感染(ARI)仍然是热带东南亚国家缅甸的一个主要公共卫生问题,但全面的分子 监测 数据有限。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 2024 年 6 月至 11 月,仰光两家医院招募了 ARI 门诊患者。我们在 2024 年雨季进行了门诊 监测 调查,并表征了病原体分布、季节性和病毒遗传多样性。
elements_zh.methods: 通过快速诊断测试 (RDT) 对鼻咽拭子进行流感、呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV) 和 SARS-CoV-2 筛查。RDT 阳性样本通过实时 PCR (RT-PCR) 进行确认。RDT 阴性样本使用 BioFire ® FilmArray ® Respiratory 2.1 Panel (BioFire RP) 进行测试。对循环阈值 (Ct) < 32 的甲型 (H1N1)pdm09、甲型 (H3N2) 和 B/维多利亚流感病毒进行了血凝素 (HA) 系统发育的新一代测序。hMPV 的部分 F 基因测序显示,基因型从 2023 年的 A2/B1 混合型转变为 2024 年的 B2 型为主。
elements_zh.main_results: 在 646 名 ARI 门诊患者(中位年龄 3.7 岁)中,548 名(84.8%)至少检测到一种病原体。在通过 BioFire RP 分析的 315 份 RDT 阴性样本中,鼻病毒/肠道病毒 (42.5%) 和 hMPV (15.2%) 最为常见。229 份 BioFire RP 阳性标本中,有 35 份 (15.3%) 被鉴定为合并感染。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 系统发育分析显示,甲型流感 (H3N2) 序列聚集在进化枝 J.2/J.2.1/J.2.2 内,B/Victoria 序列聚集在 V1A.3a.2(主要是 C.5.7)内,单个 A(H1N1)pdm09 序列聚集在 C.1.9 内。2024 年雨季期间,多种呼吸道病毒在此环境中共同传播,呈现出流感和 RSV 明显的季节性高峰。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 持续的病毒遗传 进化 强调了对持续分子 监测 的需求。研究结果强调了了解病毒传播模式对于改善公共卫生准备的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 所提供的证据并未报告与研究设计或分析方法相关的具体限制。由于该研究的观察性质和病原体检测的潜在局限性,研究结果的可信度为中等。

papers.full_text: Abstract Background The COVID-19 pandemic has altered the epidemic patterns of human metapneumovirus (hMPV) globally. As no licensed prophylactic products currently exist for hMPV, understanding population immunity is essential for identifying susceptible groups and informing prevention strategies. This study aimed to quantify age-specific hMPV neutralizing antibody (NAb) levels and seroprevalence in the postpandemic period. Methods We analyzed serum samples collected in a previously published community-based cross-sectional sero-epidemiological survey conducted in Taizhou city, eastern China, from June 2 to June 30, 2024, using a multistage, age-stratified sampling design with additional oversampling of children aged < 5 years. Serum samples were tested for hMPV NAb levels via a fluorescence-based microneutralization assay, with seropositivity defined as a titer of 1:30. We estimated geometric mean titers (GMTs) and seroprevalence rates across age groups. Factors associated with the NAb titer were examined using generalized linear models. We also examined the relationship between RSV- and hMPV-specific antibody responses, given their potential cross-reactivity. Results A total of 1303 participants aged 16 months to 93 years were included. Antibody levels were lowest among children aged 16 to < 36 months (GMT: 217, 95% CI: 159–295). The GMTs increased to 331 among children aged 3–4 years and exceeded 1000 among those aged 5–11 years, remaining elevated throughout life. The highest GMTs were observed in adults aged 65 years and older (1829, 95% CI: 1620–2064). Among children aged < 5 years, NAb titers increased by 74.7% (95% CI: 14.4%–167.0%) for each additional year of age. Approximately 67.8% (137/202) of the participants were seropositive in the age groups of 16 to < 36 months. From 6 years onward, the seroprevalence was close to or reached 100%. Higher RSV prefusion F IgG antibody titers were significantly associated with higher hMPV NAb titers (Spearman’s ρ: 0.302, P < 0.001), which may reflect shared epidemiological exposures, individual differences in immune responses, or possible cross-reactive immunity between the two viruses. Conclusions This study provides population-based evidence of age-specific hMPV NAb patterns in the post-COVID-19 pandemic period. The relatively low seroprevalence in children aged 16 to < 36 months highlights the importance of continued hMPV surveillance in this potentially susceptible population. papers.title: Association between 12 common respiratory pathogens and Streptococcus pneumoniae detection among hospitalized children in Hainan, and characterization of antimicrobial resistance and molecular epidemiology in pneumococcal isolates
papers.abstract: Data from the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated a strong association between reduced invasive pneumococcal disease and decreased circulation of specific respiratory viruses. However, studies investigating the association between common respiratory pathogens and Streptococcus pneumoniae ( S. pneumoniae ) detection rates remain limited, and molecular epidemiology data for pediatric S. pneumoniae infections in Hainan are lacking. From July 2021 to June 2025, we retrospectively analyzed the detection profiles of 12 common respiratory pathogens in hospitalized children. Spearman correlation was used to examine the relationship between each pathogen’s monthly detection rate and its co-detection rate with S. Separately, 434 consecutive S. pneumoniae isolates collected from May 2023 to April 2024 underwent Quellung serotyping, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing. During the study period, S. pneumoniae detection rates among hospitalized children in Hainan ranged from 20% to 40% without a clear seasonal pattern, but were higher during strict COVID-19 lockdowns than after policy relaxation. Positive ecological correlations were observed between S. pneumoniae detection rates and 12 common respiratory pathogen circulation. Age-stratified analysis revealed distinct correlation patterns: HMPV, IAV, RSV, and CoV showed the strongest associations with S. pneumoniae co-detection in children aged 0–3 years; M. pneumoniae , HMPV, HRV, and RSV in those aged 4–6 years; and IAV, IBV, AdV, and HMPV in those aged 7–18 years. pneumoniae isolates, 21 serotypes and 85 sequence types (24 novel) were identified. The six most prevalent serotypes were 19 F, 6B, 23 F, 19 A, 6 A, and 15 A, with ST271 as the dominant sequence type. All non-meningitis isolates were penicillin-susceptible at non-meningitis breakpoints, and serotype 19 F exhibited the highest antimicrobial resistance rates. PCV13 and PPV23 covered 78.3% and 76.5% of isolates, respectively. A 13.8% discordance rate was observed between Quellung serotyping and molecular serotyping, with discrepancies concentrated in serogroup 6. Additional discrepancies arose when molecular serotyping results were compared across different platforms. Our findings suggest that the circulation of RSV, M. pneumoniae , HMPV, HRV, and influenza viruses may influence S. pneumoniae detection in hospitalized children. These findings pertain to this clinical population and should not be extrapolated to colonization rates in healthy individuals. Finally, accurate pneumococcal surveillance in the post-vaccine era would benefit from integrating genomic and traditional phenotypic approaches.

Separately, 434 consecutive S. pneumoniae isolates collected from May 2023 to April 2024 underwent Quellung serotyping, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing. During the study period, S. pneumoniae detection rates among hospitalized children in Hainan ranged from 20% to 40% without a clear seasonal pattern, but were higher during strict COVID-19 lockdowns than after policy relaxation. papers.abstract_zh: COVID-19 大流行的数据表明,侵袭性肺炎球菌疾病减少与特定呼吸道病毒循环减少之间存在密切关联。然而,调查常见呼吸道病原体与肺炎链球菌检出率之间关系的研究仍然有限,并且缺乏海南儿童肺炎链球菌感染的分子 流行病学 数据。回顾性分析2021年7月至2025年6月住院儿童12种常见呼吸道病原体的检测情况。采用 Spearman 相关性检验每种病原体的月检出率及其与链球菌的共检出率之间的关系。另外,对 2023 年 5 月至 2024 年 4 月连续收集的 434 株肺炎链球菌分离株进行了 Quellung 血清分型、药敏检测和全 基因组 测序。研究期间,海南省住院儿童的肺炎链球菌检出率在20%至40%之间,没有明显的季节性模式,但在严格的COVID-19封锁期间比政策放松后更高。肺炎链球菌检出率与 12 种常见呼吸道病原体循环之间存在正生态相关性。年龄分层分析揭示了不同的相关模式:HMPV、IAV、RSV 和 CoV 在 0-3 岁儿童中与肺炎链球菌联合检测的关联性最强;4-6岁儿童肺炎支原体、HMPV、HRV和RSV;7-18 岁人群的 IAV、IBV、AdV 和 HMPV。肺炎链球菌分离株,已鉴定出 21 种血清型和 85 种序列类型(其中 24 种是新的)。六种最流行的血清型是 19 F、6B、23 F、19 A、6 A 和 15 A,其中 ST271 为主要序列类型。所有非脑膜炎分离株在非脑膜炎断点处均对青霉素敏感,血清型 19 F 表现出最高的抗菌素耐药率。PCV13 和 PPV23 分别覆盖了 78.3% 和 76.5% 的分离株。Quellung 血清分型和分子血清分型之间存在 13.8% 的不一致率,差异集中在血清组 6。当在不同平台上比较分子血清分型结果时,还出现了其他差异。我们的研究结果表明,RSV、肺炎支原体、HMPV、HRV 和流感病毒的传播可能会影响住院儿童中肺炎链球菌的检测。这些发现适用于该临床人群,不应推断健康个体的定植率。最后,后 疫苗 时代准确的肺炎球菌 疫苗 将受益于基因组和传统表型方法的整合。

news.content_title: Molecular Etiology and Mortality Risk Stratification of Non-SARS-CoV-2 Severe Acute Respiratory Infection in a Predominantly Pediatric Cohort: A Retrospective Study From a Tertiary Care Hospital in North India
news.content: Abstract Background: Severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) remain a major cause of hospitalization and mortality, particularly among children and other vulnerable populations. Early identification of pathogens and disease severity is essential for clinical decision-making. This study evaluated the etiology of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI and the prognostic utility of the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score) in a predominantly pediatric cohort. Methods: In this retrospective study, 117 hospitalized SARS-CoV-2-negative SARI patients, including 103 children and 14 adults, admitted to a tertiary care hospital in North India between September and December 2021 were evaluated. Respiratory pathogens were identified using multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), alongside blood and lower respiratory tract cultures. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured. Mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results: The median age was 2.0 years (interquartile range, 0.5-7.5 years). Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B predominating. Blood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%), predominantly yielding methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Overall mortality was 20.5%, increasing to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis. Elevated CRP and PCT were observed in all septic patients. The ViVI Score showed excellent mortality prediction (area under the curve (AUC) 0.946). A cutoff of ≥30 yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity and was strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001). Conclusion: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, whereas bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. Multiplex molecular diagnostics combined with standardized severity assessment may improve clinical triage, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings. Introduction Severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) pose a significant global health challenge, causing substantial morbidity and mortality, particularly among vulnerable populations. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines SARI as an acute respiratory illness with a history of fever or measured fever of ≥38°C and cough, with onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization [1]. However, this syndromic definition does not provide information regarding the underlying etiological agent or the individual risk of adverse outcomes. SARI may result from a wide range of viral and bacterial pathogens, and conventional diagnostic methods may not always provide a timely or comprehensive etiological diagnosis. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, SARI detection was largely syndromic, relying on clinical presentation and limited diagnostic capacity [2]. The pandemic acted as a catalyst for strengthening surveillance systems and pathogen identification. In India, surveillance of epidemic-prone diseases is supported through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, including laboratory-based and information technology-enabled surveillance [3]. SARI constitutes a major cause of healthcare utilization and hospitalization and may require referral to secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities, particularly among young children, older adults, and individuals with underlying comorbidities. Family physicians are often the first point of contact for patients presenting with acute respiratory symptoms and therefore play a pivotal role in early recognition of severe disease, timely referral, initiation of appropriate management, and implementation of infection prevention measures [1,2]. Accurate identification of respiratory pathogens and early risk stratification are essential to improve patient outcomes while minimizing unnecessary antibiotic use [2]. In low- and middle-income countries such as India, access to specialized diagnostic services remains limited at primary-care facilities, with sample transport and referral mechanisms used to improve access to diagnostic testing [4]. Consequently, evidence on the etiological profile of SARI and validated clinical severity assessment tools is highly relevant for strengthening referral pathways, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory disease surveillance. Such evidence can assist family physicians and primary care providers in identifying patients requiring urgent referral, promoting rational antimicrobial use, and optimizing utilization of healthcare resources [2,4]. To standardize clinical assessment, various severity scoring systems have been introduced. One of the most widely recognized is the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score), developed by the Vienna Vaccine Safety Initiative. This 22-item composite score quantifies the clinical severity of influenza-like illnesses and SARI across diverse patient populations [5]. It includes indicators of both uncomplicated and complicated disease, providing a standardized framework for clinical decision-making, disease severity assessment, and epidemiological comparison. The advent of multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) platforms has markedly advanced the diagnostic approach to SARI by enabling simultaneous detection of multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy and expediting clinical decision-making [6]. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment has the potential to improve clinical risk stratification while strengthening pathogen-specific surveillance and facilitating the integration of virological and clinical data for surveillance and public health applications [6,7]. Despite advances in molecular diagnostics and standardized severity assessment, evidence integrating pathogen identification with clinical risk stratification in non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI remains limited, particularly from resource-constrained settings. Addressing this gap may help strengthen clinical decision-making, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory infection surveillance across primary and tertiary healthcare settings. Materials & Methods Study design and setting This retrospective observational study analyzed laboratory and clinical data of patients admitted with severe acute respiratory syndrome during the defined period from September to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. The data analysis was undertaken subsequently in the post-pandemic phase. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India (Approval Ref No. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Cert./05-2024/54, dated 23/07/2024). The primary objective was to establish an etiological profile of pathogens responsible for SARI other than SARS-CoV-2 among hospitalized patients, using a combination of multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture. Clinical and laboratory data were retrieved retrospectively from hospital records. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. Sampling technique and patient selection Consecutive patients admitted during the study period with signs and symptoms of acute respiratory illness were screened for inclusion. Patients meeting the WHO SARI case definition, with fever ≥38°C and cough, with symptom onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization, were included in the study [1]. The study cohort comprised predominantly pediatric patients, with 103 children and 14 adults. Pathogen detection and laboratory methods RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 Nasopharyngeal and/or oropharyngeal swabs were collected from all SARI patients in the hospital during that period and tested for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Patients who tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 were included in this study and were subjected to multiplex PCR. Testing was performed in a designated COVID-19 molecular diagnostic laboratory, following Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidelines [8] and using ICMR-National Institute of Virology-approved commercial RT-PCR kits. The test targeted specific viral genes (e.g., E, ORF) for detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA. Multiplex PCR for Respiratory Pathogens Respiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal/throat swabs) were further subjected to multiplex PCR using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg). This assay detects Chlamydia pneumoniae, Enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae B, Human adenovirus, Human bocavirus, Human coronavirus 229E, Human coronavirus HKU1, Human coronavirus NL63, Human coronavirus OC43, Human metapneumoviruses A/B, Human parainfluenza virus 1-4, Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B, Human rhinovirus, Influenza A virus, Influenza A (H1N1) virus, Influenza B virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Tests were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol, including appropriate internal and external controls. Conventional Microbiological Culture Blood cultures were performed in all 117 enrolled patients using the BacT/ALERT® automated system (bioMérieux, France). Samples that flagged positive were subcultured on blood and MacConkey agar plates, followed by identification using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Patients with positive blood cultures were clinically evaluated and classified as having sepsis based on the treating clinical team's assessment and documented clinical findings. All 40 patients with positive blood cultures were clinically diagnosed with sepsis. The lower respiratory tract samples were processed using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Isolates were identified by morphology, Gram staining, and biochemical profiling. Biomarkers Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured on the Mispa i3 automated cartridge-based specific protein analyser (Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kerala, India). The platform uses a dual-channel system (rate-based nephelometry and turbidimetry/photometry) and prefilled single-use reagent cartridges with test-specific IC-card (smart card) calibration. Disease severity assessment The ViVI Score was used to assess disease severity based on 22 clinical parameters, with a total score ranging from 0 to 48 [11,12]. The scoring was weighted as follows: Disease Severity with Uncomplicated Symptoms (DSU): Weight=1×; Disease Severity with Complicated Symptoms (DSC): Weight=3×; Total Disease Severity Score=DSU + DSC. A schematic representation of the study methodology is shown in Figure 1. Statistical analysis Pathogen distributions and descriptive statistics (median, IQR) were calculated in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, United States), and odds ratios were estimated using Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance of the ViVI Score for outcome classification was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of ordinal rating data in JROCFIT v2.0.1 (John Eng; based on ROCFIT by Metz et al.) [13]: outcomes were coded as positive = survival (alive) and negative = death, ViVI scores were converted into an ordinal rating scale in which higher categories represented stronger evidence of the positive state, and a maximum-likelihood unequal-variance binormal ROC model was fitted to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its standard deviation; because ViVI is a severity index (higher scores indicate poorer prognosis), the ratings were oriented such that lower ViVI scores corresponded to stronger evidence of survival. Results A total of 117 patients were included in the study. The cohort was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. The median age of the study population was 2.0 years (IQR 0.5-7.5 years). The male-to-female ratio was 1.81:1, indicating a male predominance. Pathogen detection profile from the multiplex PCR Out of the 117 patients, 81 (69.2%) were positive for at least one respiratory pathogen using multiplex PCR. Multiplex respiratory pathogen testing identified HRSV A/B as the most frequently detected pathogen (n=60), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=16), Staphylococcus aureus (n=11), human rhinovirus (n=8), and influenza B virus (n=7). Lower detection rates were observed for human parainfluenza virus type 4 (n=3), human adenovirus (n=2), human coronavirus OC43, human metapneumovirus A/B, human parainfluenza virus type 3, and human parechovirus (each n=1). No cases were detected for Chlamydophila pneumoniae, enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, human bocavirus, human coronaviruses 229E, HKU1, and NL63, human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2, influenza A virus (including H1N1), or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Conversely, 36 patients tested negative for all pathogens, indicating either non-infectious etiologies or undetected organisms outside the panel’s scope (Figure 2). Additionally, six cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) due to HRSV were documented in a subset of adult patients, along with HRSV positivity among 13 children with underlying hematological disorders. Pathogen detection profile from conventional cultures Blood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%); five were adults, and 35 were children. Among the positive blood cultures, 18 yielded methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, seven Escherichia coli, seven Klebsiella pneumoniae, seven Streptococcus pneumoniae, and one yielded both S. aureus and S. pneumoniae. Lower respiratory tract aerobic cultures were positive in 48 patients (five adults and 43 children), yielding S. pneumoniae in 15, E. coli in 12, confluent growth of K. pneumoniae in 10, and S. aureus in 10; one patient had both S. pneumoniae and S. aureus. Biomarker profile Elevated PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) was observed in 55/117 patients (47.0%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Markedly elevated CRP (>10 mg/dL) was observed in 101/117 patients (86.3%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Positive D-dimer, suggestive of a hypercoagulable state, was observed in 35 patients, of whom 30 had sepsis. ViVI Score distribution The median ViVI Score across all patients was 22. Distribution of ViVI scores varied based on pathogen and infection type. Among single infections, HRSV A/B was most frequent (n=38) with a median ViVI score of 20.5 (IQR 13.5). Other single pathogens were less common, including Staphylococcus aureus (n=5; median 20 (IQR 19)), Influenza B (n=4; median 20.5 (IQR 10.25)), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=3; median 29 (IQR 6.5)), Human rhinovirus (n=2; median 35 (IQR 6)), and individual cases of adenovirus (median 37) and parainfluenza virus 4 (median 42). Among coinfections, HRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most common (n=10; median 21 (IQR 13.75)). Other HRSV coinfections included HRSV + rhinovirus (n=3; median 20 (IQR 4)), HRSV + Influenza B (n=2; median 32 (IQR 16)), and HRSV + Staphylococcus aureus (n=2; median 20 (IQR 3)), while the remaining coinfections occurred as single cases with variable ViVI scores (Table 1). Clinical outcomes and mortality The overall mortality rate in the cohort was 20.5% (24/117). Of particular concern was the subgroup of patients presenting with SARI and culture-confirmed sepsis (n=40), in which mortality rose dramatically to 60% (24/40). This suggests that progression to sepsis remains the strongest indicator of poor outcomes in SARI cases. Predictive utility of the ViVI Score A total of 117 cases were analyzed (93 survivors and 24 deaths). ROC analysis using JROCFIT demonstrated excellent discrimination between survivors and non-survivors (fitted AUC 0.946 (SD 0.022); empiric AUC 0.942) (Figure 3). The ROC curve lies close to the upper-left corner, indicating excellent discriminatory performance of the ViVI Score for predicting mortality across a range of decision thresholds (Figure 3). Using the ViVI Score as a mortality predictor and classifying death as the event, a low cutoff of ViVI ≥15 yielded 100% sensitivity for death (24/24) but low specificity (29.0%, 27/93) (TP=24, FN=0, TN=27, FP=66). In contrast, a high cutoff of ViVI ≥45 yielded 100% specificity (93/93) but low sensitivity (25.0%, 6/24) (TP=6, FN=18, TN=93, FP=0). The optimal threshold by Youden's J was ViVI ≥30, which provided balanced performance (sensitivity 83.3% (20/24) and specificity 91.4% (85/93); overall accuracy 89.7% (105/117)) (TP=20, FN=4, TN=85, FP=8). Patients with ViVI ≥30 had markedly increased odds of death compared with those with ViVI <30 (odds ratio 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; Fisher's exact test p=1.4 × 10−12). Discussion The present study provides a comprehensive etiological and clinical profile of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in a predominantly pediatric cohort, with simultaneous assessment of respiratory pathogens, bacterial culture results, inflammatory biomarkers, and disease severity. Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, while HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen. Culture-confirmed bloodstream infection was associated with substantially higher mortality, and the ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality. The 69.2% pathogen detection rate observed with multiplex PCR is consistent with previous studies demonstrating substantial pathogen detection among patients with severe respiratory infection. El Kholy et al. reported a high rate of viral detection and frequent co-detection in children with SARI, while Contier et al. demonstrated the diagnostic performance of multiplex PCR among critically ill immunocompromised patients [14,15]. Differences in age distribution, disease severity, sampling practices, seasonality, and the respiratory pathogen panels used may account for variations in diagnostic yield between studies. HRSV A/B…

Family physicians are often the first point of contact for patients presenting with acute respiratory symptoms and therefore play a pivotal role in early recognition of severe disease, timely referral, initiation of appropriate management, and implementation of infection prevention measures [1,2]. Accurate identification of respiratory pathogens and early risk stratification are essential to improve patient outcomes while minimizing unnecessary antibiotic use [2]. In low- and middle-income countries such as India, access to specialized diagnostic services remains limited at primary-care facilities, with sample transport and referral mechanisms used to improve access to diagnostic testing [4]. Consequently, evidence on the etiological profile of SARI and validated clinical severity assessment tools is highly relevant for strengthening referral pathways, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory disease surveillance. Such evidence can assist family physicians and primary care providers in identifying patients requiring urgent referral, promoting rational antimicrobial use, and optimizing utilization of healthcare resources [2,4]. To standardize clinical assessment, various severity scoring systems have been introduced. One of the most widely recognized is the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score), developed by the Vienna Vaccine Safety Initiative. This 22-item composite score quantifies the clinical severity of influenza-like illnesses and SARI across diverse patient populations [5]. It includes indicators of both uncomplicated and complicated disease, providing a standardized framework for clinical decision-making, disease severity assessment, and epidemiological comparison. The advent of multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) platforms has markedly advanced the diagnostic approach to SARI by enabling simultaneous detection of multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy and expediting clinical decision-making [6]. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment has the potential to improve clinical risk stratification while strengthening pathogen-specific surveillance and facilitating the integration of virological and clinical data for surveillance and public health applications [6,7]. Despite advances in molecular diagnostics and standardized severity assessment, evidence integrating pathogen identification with clinical risk stratification in non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI remains limited, particularly from resource-constrained settings. Addressing this gap may help strengthen clinical decision-making, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory infection surveillance across primary and tertiary healthcare settings. Materials & Methods Study design and setting This retrospective observational study analyzed laboratory and clinical data of patients admitted with severe acute respiratory syndrome during the defined period from September to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. The data analysis was undertaken subsequently in the post-pandemic phase. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India (Approval Ref No. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Cert./05-2024/54, dated 23/07/2024). The primary objective was to establish an etiological profile of pathogens responsible for SARI other than SARS-CoV-2 among hospitalized patients, using a combination of multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture. Clinical and laboratory data were retrieved retrospectively from hospital records. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. Sampling technique and patient selection Consecutive patients admitted during the study period with signs and symptoms of acute respiratory illness were screened for inclusion. Patients meeting the WHO SARI case definition, with fever ≥38°C and cough, with symptom onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization, were included in the study [1]. The study cohort comprised predominantly pediatric patients, with 103 children and 14 adults. Pathogen detection and laboratory methods RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 Nasopharyngeal and/or oropharyngeal swabs were collected from all SARI patients in the hospital during that period and tested for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Patients who tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 were included in this study and were subjected to multiplex PCR. Testing was performed in a designated COVID-19 molecular diagnostic laboratory, following Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidelines [8] and using ICMR-National Institute of Virology-approved commercial RT-PCR kits. The test targeted specific viral genes (e.g., E, ORF) for detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA. Multiplex PCR for Respiratory Pathogens Respiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal/throat swabs) were further subjected to multiplex PCR using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg). This assay detects Chlamydia pneumoniae, Enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae B, Human adenovirus, Human bocavirus, Human coronavirus 229E, Human coronavirus HKU1, Human coronavirus NL63, Human coronavirus OC43, Human metapneumoviruses A/B, Human parainfluenza virus 1-4, Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B, Human rhinovirus, Influenza A virus, Influenza A (H1N1) virus, Influenza B virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Tests were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol, including appropriate internal and external controls. Conventional Microbiological Culture Blood cultures were performed in all 117 enrolled patients using the BacT/ALERT® automated system (bioMérieux, France). Samples that flagged positive were subcultured on blood and MacConkey agar plates, followed by identification using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Patients with positive blood cultures were clinically evaluated and classified as having sepsis based on the treating clinical team's assessment and documented clinical findings. All 40 patients with positive blood cultures were clinically diagnosed with sepsis. The lower respiratory tract samples were processed using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Isolates were identified by morphology, Gram staining, and biochemical profiling. Biomarkers Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured on the Mispa i3 automated cartridge-based specific protein analyser (Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kerala, India). The platform uses a dual-channel system (rate-based nephelometry and turbidimetry/photometry) and prefilled single-use reagent cartridges with test-specific IC-card (smart card) calibration. Disease severity assessment The ViVI Score was used to assess disease severity based on 22 clinical parameters, with a total score ranging from 0 to 48 [11,12]. The scoring was weighted as follows: Disease Severity with Uncomplicated Symptoms (DSU): Weight=1×; Disease Severity with Complicated Symptoms (DSC): Weight=3×; Total Disease Severity Score=DSU + DSC. A schematic representation of the study methodology is shown in Figure 1. Statistical analysis Pathogen distributions and descriptive statistics (median, IQR) were calculated in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, United States), and odds ratios were estimated using Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance of the ViVI Score for outcome classification was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of ordinal rating data in JROCFIT v2.0.1 (John Eng; based on ROCFIT by Metz et al.) [13]: outcomes were coded as positive = survival (alive) and negative = death, ViVI scores were converted into an ordinal rating scale in which higher categories represented stronger evidence of the positive state, and a maximum-likelihood unequal-variance binormal ROC model was fitted to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its standard deviation; because ViVI is a severity index (higher scores indicate poorer prognosis), the ratings were oriented such that lower ViVI scores corresponded to stronger evidence of survival. Results A total of 117 patients were included in the study. The cohort was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. The median age of the study population was 2.0 years (IQR 0.5-7.5 years). The male-to-female ratio was 1.81:1, indicating a male predominance. Pathogen detection profile from the multiplex PCR Out of the 117 patients, 81 (69.2%) were positive for at least one respiratory pathogen using multiplex PCR. Multiplex respiratory pathogen testing identified HRSV A/B as the most frequently detected pathogen (n=60), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=16), Staphylococcus aureus (n=11), human rhinovirus (n=8), and influenza B virus (n=7). Lower detection rates were observed for human parainfluenza virus type 4 (n=3), human adenovirus (n=2), human coronavirus OC43, human metapneumovirus A/B, human parainfluenza virus type 3, and human parechovirus (each n=1). No cases were detected for Chlamydophila pneumoniae, enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, human bocavirus, human coronaviruses 229E, HKU1, and NL63, human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2, influenza A virus (including H1N1), or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Conversely, 36 patients tested negative for all pathogens, indicating either non-infectious etiologies or undetected organisms outside the panel’s scope (Figure 2). Additionally, six cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) due to HRSV were documented in a subset of adult patients, along with HRSV positivity among 13 children with underlying hematological disorders. Pathogen detection profile from conventional cultures Blood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%); five were adults, and 35 were children. Among the positive blood cultures, 18 yielded methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, seven Escherichia coli, seven Klebsiella pneumoniae, seven Streptococcus pneumoniae, and one yielded both S. aureus and S. pneumoniae. Lower respiratory tract aerobic cultures were positive in 48 patients (five adults and 43 children), yielding S. pneumoniae in 15, E. coli in 12, confluent growth of K. pneumoniae in 10, and S. aureus in 10; one patient had both S. pneumoniae and S. aureus. Biomarker profile Elevated PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) was observed in 55/117 patients (47.0%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Markedly elevated CRP (>10 mg/dL) was observed in 101/117 patients (86.3%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Positive D-dimer, suggestive of a hypercoagulable state, was observed in 35 patients, of whom 30 had sepsis. ViVI Score distribution The median ViVI Score across all patients was 22. Distribution of ViVI scores varied based on pathogen and infection type. Among single infections, HRSV A/B was most frequent (n=38) with a median ViVI score of 20.5 (IQR 13.5). Other single pathogens were less common, including Staphylococcus aureus (n=5; median 20 (IQR 19)), Influenza B (n=4; median 20.5 (IQR 10.25)), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=3; median 29 (IQR 6.5)), Human rhinovirus (n=2; median 35 (IQR 6)), and individual cases of adenovirus (median 37) and parainfluenza virus 4 (median 42). Among coinfections, HRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most common (n=10; median 21 (IQR 13.75)). Other HRSV coinfections included HRSV + rhinovirus (n=3; median 20 (IQR 4)), HRSV + Influenza B (n=2; median 32 (IQR 16)), and HRSV + Staphylococcus aureus (n=2; median 20 (IQR 3)), while the remaining coinfections occurred as single cases with variable ViVI scores (Table 1). Clinical outcomes and mortality The overall mortality rate in the cohort was 20.5% (24/117). Of particular concern was the subgroup of patients presenting with SARI and culture-confirmed sepsis (n=40), in which mortality rose dramatically to 60% (24/40). This suggests that progression to sepsis remains the strongest indicator of poor outcomes in SARI cases. Predictive utility of the ViVI Score A total of 117 cases were analyzed (93 survivors and 24 deaths). ROC analysis using JROCFIT demonstrated excellent discrimination between survivors and non-survivors (fitted AUC 0.946 (SD 0.022); empiric AUC 0.942) (Figure 3). The ROC curve lies close to the upper-left corner, indicating excellent discriminatory performance of the ViVI Score for predicting mortality across a range of decision thresholds (Figure 3). Using the ViVI Score as a mortality predictor and classifying death as the event, a low cutoff of ViVI ≥15 yielded 100% sensitivity for death (24/24) but low specificity (29.0%, 27/93) (TP=24, FN=0, TN=27, FP=66). In contrast, a high cutoff of ViVI ≥45 yielded 100% specificity (93/93) but low sensitivity (25.0%, 6/24) (TP=6, FN=18, TN=93, FP=0). The optimal threshold by Youden's J was ViVI ≥30, which provided balanced performance (sensitivity 83.3% (20/24) and specificity 91.4% (85/93); overall accuracy 89.7% (105/117)) (TP=20, FN=4, TN=85, FP=8). Patients with ViVI ≥30 had markedly increased odds of death compared with those with ViVI <30 (odds ratio 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; Fisher's exact test p=1.4 × 10−12). Discussion The present study provides a comprehensive etiological and clinical profile of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in a predominantly pediatric cohort, with simultaneous assessment of respiratory pathogens, bacterial culture results, inflammatory biomarkers, and disease severity. Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, while HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen. Culture-confirmed bloodstream infection was associated with substantially higher mortality, and the ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality. The 69.2% pathogen detection rate observed with multiplex PCR is consistent with previous studies demonstrating substantial pathogen detection among patients with severe respiratory infection. El Kholy et al. reported a high rate of viral detection and frequent co-detection in children with SARI, while Contier et al. demonstrated the diagnostic performance of multiplex PCR among critically ill immunocompromised patients [14,15]. Differences in age distribution, disease severity, sampling practices, seasonality, and the respiratory pathogen panels used may account for variations in diagnostic yield between studies. analysis.brief_en: This retrospective study from a tertiary care hospital in North India analyzed non-SARS-CoV-2 severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) in 117 hospitalized patients, including 103 children and 14 adults, admitted between September and December 2021. Overall mortality was 20.5%, rising to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis. The study highlights the importance of accurate pathogen identification and early risk stratification to improve patient outcomes and reduce unnecessary antibiotic use, especially in resource-limited settings like India. The findings suggest that integrating rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment tools could enhance clinical decision-making and respiratory disease surveillance.

news.title_zh: 以儿科为主的 死亡率 非 SARS-CoV-2 严重急性呼吸道感染的分子病因学和 死亡率 风险分层:印度北部一家三级护理医院的回顾性研究 - Cureus
news.source_body_en: This retrospective study from a tertiary care hospital in North India analyzed non-SARS-CoV-2 severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) in 117 hospitalized patients, including 103 children and 14 adults, admitted between September and December 2021. news.content_zh: 这项来自印度北部一家三级护理医院的回顾性研究分析了 2021 年 9 月至 12 月期间收治的 117 名住院患者(包括 103 名儿童和 14 名成人)的非 SARS-CoV-2 严重急性呼吸道感染 (SARI)。该研究旨在评估 SARI 的病因以及 ViVI 疾病严重程度评分 (ViVI 评分) 在以儿科为主的 队列研究 中的预后价值。使用多重 PCR 和常规微生物培养,鉴定出呼吸道病原体,其中人呼吸道合胞病毒 (HRSV) A/B 占主导地位。34.2%的患者血培养呈阳性,大部分为甲氧西林敏感金黄色葡萄球菌。总体 死亡率 为 20.5%,在培养确诊的脓毒症患者中上升至 60%。ViVI 评分表现出出色的 死亡率 预测 (AUC 0.946),截止值≥30,显示出 83.3% 的敏感性和 91.4% 的特异性。该研究强调了准确的病原体识别和早期风险分层对于改善患者治疗结果和减少不必要的抗生素使用的重要性,特别是在印度等资源有限的地区。研究结果表明,将快速分子诊断与标准化严重程度评估工具相结合可以增强临床决策和呼吸系统疾病 监测。
